source.title: Ring-Zero: Scaling Zero RL to a Trillion Parameters for Emergent Reasoning
source.authors: Xin-Yu Tang; Qian Cao; Yu-Rou Liu; Yu-Liang Zhan; Xiao-Chong Lan; Yi-Fan Li; Yuchen Yan; Han Peng; Zi-Can Dong; Zhen-Duo Zhang; Tianshu Wang; Xinyu Kong; Zu-Jie Wen; Wayne Xin Zhao; Zhi-Qiang Zhang; Jun Zhou

record.tranche_reason: It compares mathematical benchmark performance across model sizes, bearing on downstream performance versus scale, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit a scaling law.
record.gate_note: The study reports no held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits, loss extrapolations, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its relevant results are the two explicitly reported AIME comparisons between the 104B and 1T models; other benchmark values in the flattened table are not assigned where the layout does not support reliable matching.
record.test_reason: The study is about zero-RL post-training of two MoE models (104B and 1T total parameters). Its only scale result is a two-point comparison of AIME accuracy after RL, taken at unequal step counts (3,600 vs 5,200). It fits no power law and reports no pretraining loss or compute-optimal split. Two sizes cannot show the 'predictable' improvement V6 names. The result is a related but different finding: larger base models benefit more from zero RL.
record.authors_conclusion: Roughly right. The authors conclude that scaling from 104B to 1T parameters raises the zero-RL performance ceiling and sample efficiency, framed as a 'bitter lesson' validation. They also claim that emergent behaviours at 1T make hand-crafted rewards redundant. They make no claim about power-law or predictable scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models with zero-RL and evaluates mathematical reasoning accuracy; it does not use the original held-out-loss scaling-law measurement or fit loss curves.

fits_no_version.finding: After zero-RL training, the 1T MoE (63B active) beats the 104B MoE (7.4B active) on AIME 2024 (89.06 vs 71.72) and AIME 2025 (83.28 vs 63.54). The 104B model had more RL steps. The gap is reported to widen on harder benchmarks (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger base models gain more from zero-RL post-training on math reasoning, in both ceiling and sample efficiency.

record.problems: The relevant scale comparison includes only two model sizes and reports different training-step counts. No uncertainty estimates or held-out pretraining-loss measurements are provided.
record.rows_left_out: Other benchmark results in Table 1 were not extracted because the flattened table layout does not reliably associate all displayed values with their model and benchmark columns.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fitted laws and no extrapolation.
No shape ablations at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in the RL regime; only two sizes.
Predictability across scale and the relation to pretraining loss are untested; only two post-RL model sizes are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and V6 'supports' overreach. The scale result is two points, both after RL post-training, at unequal step counts, with no fit, so it cannot bear on predictable scaling. Table 1 also lists Ring-2.5-flash-Zero (First Stage RL) at 71.2 on AIME 2024, but that table's columns are hard to align.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study compares downstream math accuracy at only two model sizes; it does not test a predictive relationship across a broad scale range or relate downstream performance to pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Ring-2.5-1T-Zero-I

rows.locator: Section 5.1, How Much Does Model Size Affect Training?
rows.note: The text reports the 1T model's score after 3,600 steps and the 104B model's score even after 5,200 steps; training steps therefore differ.
rows.check: Two-size comparison of post-RL AIME 2024 accuracy at different step counts (1T at 3,600 vs 104B at 5,200). It cannot show predictable scaling; the baseline is a different model at a different step, not a scaling-law prediction.
